claims.text: A two-phase coexistence simulation at the DFT level will reliably predict melting temperature for refractory materials.
The proposed simulation will reliably predict entropy of fusion.
The proposed simulation will reliably predict enthalpy of fusion.
The proposed simulation will reliably predict volume change at the melting point.
The proposed approach will drastically reduce computational cost relative to full thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamics.
The modeled initial state contains both solid and liquid phases near melting.
Interface pinning and the Z method are examples of two-phase coexistence methods usable under DFT-level conditions.
Solid and liquid phases coexist in equilibrium near the melting point.
The solid-liquid interface mediates the melting transition.
Direct equilibrium simulation of coexisting phases permits extraction of thermodynamic differences across the solid-liquid interface.
Thermodynamic differences extracted across the interface determine melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and melting-volume change.
Direct coexistence simulation avoids extensive integration over thermodynamic paths.
The computational-cost reduction will enable high-throughput calculations.
The conventional ab initio free-energy approach requires expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamics.
Complex phase transitions may limit the proposed method.
The method may be limited when the coexistence interface does not capture all melting phenomena.
The preservation of DFT-level accuracy across diverse refractory materials requires further validation.

contradictions.description: The intervention presents both interface pinning and the Z method as implementations of a two-phase coexistence approach, while the other fields require an initially coexisting solid-liquid state and an explicit interface. The hypothesis does not reconcile how both named alternatives satisfy that interface-based setup and mechanism.
